newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angolan soldiers reported wounded in diamond areas.
newsitem.headline: Angolan soldiers reported wounded in diamond areas.

text.p: The Angolan army has pushed deeper into diamond-rich areas held by UNITA former rebels in the northeast and at least 65 soldiers have been wounded in clashes, a military source said on Thursday.
"We can confirm at least 65 FAA (Angolan Armed Forces) casualties, but those are only the ones we have seen. We have got no idea of the number of dead," the source told Reuters.
He added that fighting was continuing to the south of Nzage.

The Luanda government said its operation was intended to flush out armed refugees who had come across the border from the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire, but analysts said this was a pretext to retake diamond-rich territory under the control of the UNITA former rebels.
The government action has sparked new clashes between the two sides which signed a peace treaty in 1994 to end a 20-year civil war.
The United Nations is implementing a to ensure peace in the southern African country, but analysts said the new tensions brought the treaty's long-term success into question in the diamond area.
Several foreign mining companies have suspended operations in Lunda Norte province because of the instability.
Since the signing of the peace pact both sides have formed a unity government and integrated their armies, although over 50,000 UNITA troops are still in U.N. assembly camps awaiting demobilisation.
A UNITA official told Reuters on Thursday the movement had suspended the handover of territory under its control to the government because of problems.
The state is meant to assume administrative control of all of the country under terms of the 1994 peace treaty.
But the process had ground to a halt, said Isaias Samakuva, UNITA's representative to the body overseeing the peace process.
"There are just too many problems at the moment," he said, without giving details.

"We have assessed the situation and have decided to suspend the process for a time while we talk with Bailundo about what to do next," he said, referring to the central highlands city where UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi keeps his headquarters.
There was no immediate response from the government.
Some estimates put the area under UNITA control at up to 70 percent of the countryside, including the diamond areas which provide the movement with up to $600 million annually.
The fall of Mobutu Sese Seko's government in the former Zaire in May was a major blow to UNITA, which had used the country as its weapons and supplies base.
The former rebels began allowing the state to re-establish administrations in some places after April 30 and the process began with the handover of M'Banza Congo in the northwest.
But UNITA supporters have ripped down state flags there several times, as they have in cities in the central highlands.
Samakuva and several government officials were badly beaten by UNITA supporters at a handover ceremony in Quibala, about 200 km (125 miles) southeast of Luanda on May 30.
"People in Angola have been separated for a very long time," said Samakuva. "They do not understand this change that is taking place, and many of them do not like it."
